The user wants a breakdown of a disaggregated prefill/decode cluster under frontend pressure, covering request routing, queueing, tail latency, cache transfer, role switching, batch completion, GPU utilization, and throughput tradeoffs. They've asked this multiple times, so maybe they need a structured answer each time.

First, I need to recall how prefill/decode works. Prefill usually refers to pre-processing data before decoding, and decode is the actual processing. Disaggregated means the components are separate, so there's no shared memory or resources. Under frontend pressure, the frontend is handling a lot of requests, so the cluster needs to handle that efficiently.

Starting with request routing. When a request arrives, it's routed to the appropriate prefill or decode module. The routing depends on the module's priority, which could be based on latency, throughput, or other factors. Maybe the frontend uses a queueing system to manage incoming requests, ensuring that each request gets processed in order.

Queueing is important here. The frontend might use a queue to manage incoming requests, which can be a FIFO (first-in, first-out) or a priority queue. The queueing system needs to handle the load, ensuring that the most urgent requests are processed first. If the queue is too long, it could lead to delays.

Tail latency refers to the time it takes for the tail of the queue to process the last request. If the queue is too long, the tail might be delayed, affecting the overall performance. The frontend needs to manage the queue size to avoid this.
